statements.claim: Vidura came to Panchala as a messenger from Hastinapura, raising the question of whether the sons of Pandu would press their claim to their ancestral kingdom.
statements.evidence: Index/evt_0406: 'At Vidura's visit...'; MB 1.209 (Viduragamana Parva) opens with Drupada answering Vidura's words ('Hearing these words of Vidura'); Drupada calls it their 'ancestral kingdom'.

statements.claim: Drupada said the princes should return to their ancestral kingdom — it was highly proper — but that it was not proper for him, their host, to say so himself; he made it conditional on the brothers desiring to go and on Balarama and Krishna being of the same mind.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: Drupada: 'It is highly proper that these illustrious princes should return to their ancestral kingdom. But it is not proper for me to say this myself. If the brave son of Kunti viz., Yudhishthira, if Bhima and Arjuna... and if Rama (Valadeva) and Krishna... be of the same mind, then let the Pandavas go thither.'

statements.claim: Drupada added that Rama and Krishna were ever engaged in doing what was agreeable and beneficial to Pandu's sons.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'For these tigers among men (Rama and Krishna) are ever engaged in doing what is agreeable and beneficial to the sons of Pandu.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira replied, 'We are now, O monarch, with all our younger brothers, dependent on thee. We shall cheerfully do what thou art pleased to command.'
statements.evidence: Verbatim in MB 1.209.

statements.claim: Krishna then gave his opinion: 'I am of opinion that the Pandavas should go. But we should all abide by the opinion of king Drupada, who is conversant with every rule of morality.'
statements.evidence: Verbatim in MB 1.209: 'Then Vasudeva said...' (also quoted in the pack's excerpt).

statements.claim: Drupada agreed with Krishna's judgment, saying the sons of Pandu were now as dear to him as to Vasudeva, and paid the tribute: 'Kunti's son Yudhishthira himself doth not seek the welfare of the Pandavas so earnestly as, Kesava, that tiger among men.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Drupada then spoke, I certainly agree... Kunti's son Yudhishthira himself doth not seek the welfare of the Pandavas so earnestly as, Kesava...' — spoken by Drupada, as the story has it.

statements.claim: Commanded by Drupada, the Pandavas with Krishna and Vidura set out, taking Draupadi and the renowned Kunti, journeying toward the city called after the elephant (Hastinapura), stopping along the way for pleasure and enjoyment.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Commanded by the illustrious Drupada, the Pandavas... and Krishna and Vidura, taking with them Krishna, the daughter of Drupada, and the renowned Kunti, journeyed towards the city called after the elephant, stopping at various places along the way for purposes of pleasure and enjoyment.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra sent out the Kauravas Vikarna, Chitrasena, Drona and Kripa to receive the heroes, and the citizens of Hastinapura acclaimed them, including the cries 'Here returns that tiger among men...' and the wish that the Pandavas stay in their town for a hundred years.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209 names Vikarna, Chitrasena, Drona and Kripa as sent out; both citizen cries quoted appear verbatim.

statements.claim: The Pandavas worshipped the feet of Dhritarashtra and Bhishma, enquired after the citizens' welfare, rested, and were summoned to the court, where Dhritarashtra granted them Khandavaprastha with half the kingdom: 'Repair ye to Khandavaprastha so that no difference may arise again... Protected by Partha (Arjuna)... taking half of the kingdom.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: summoned by Dhritarashtra and Bhishma; Dhritarashtra's address to Yudhishthira quoted verbatim.

statements.claim: Content with half a kingdom, the brothers worshipped the king and set out from Hastinapura to Khandavaprastha, which lay in unreclaimed desert.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Agreeing to what Dhritarashtra said... they removed to Khandavaprastha, which was in unreclaimed desert.'

statements.claim: Krishna, who had counselled the return, was already thinking ahead to what the desert land could become (staying on with them).
statements.evidence: Foreshadowing of 1.209's continuation ('with Krishna at their head, arriving there'); forward-looking connective close, not a discrete sourceable fact in the passage.

notes: All substantive claims (Vidura's visit, Drupada's conditional assent, Yudhishthira's and Krishna's speeches, Drupada's tribute, the journey, the reception, the Khandavaprastha grant) match MB 1.209 closely, several verbatim. Closing foreshadowing is connective.

statements.claim: The land Dhritarashtra granted the Pandavas, Khandavaprastha, was unreclaimed desert — thorn, dust and emptiness, with no city yet raised.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'they removed to Khandavaprastha, which was in unreclaimed desert'; index summary: Krishna helps establish Indraprastha there.

statements.claim: The brothers came content, asking only that no difference should arise again between them and their cousins.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: Dhritarashtra's words 'so that no difference may arise again (between you and your cousins)' and the brothers' agreement.

statements.claim: Krishna did not go home: he came with them into the wilderness and stayed — the Pandavas worked 'with Krishna at their head'.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'Then those heroes... with Krishna at their head, arriving there, beautified the place'; pack excerpt: 'having settled the Pandavas there, the heroic Krishna... came back... to Dwaravati' only afterwards.

statements.claim: Selecting a sacred and auspicious region with the assistance of the sage Dwaipayana (Vyasa), they performed propitiatory ceremonies and measured out the piece of land for their city.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'those mighty car-warriors, selecting with Dwaipayana's assistance a sacred and auspicious region, performed certain propitiatory ceremonies and measured out a piece of land for their city.'

statements.claim: A trench was dug around the city wide as the sea, and walls rose high as the heavens, white as fleecy clouds or the rays of the moon; the city looked resplendent like Bhogavati decked with the Nagas.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'surrounded by a trench wide as the sea and by walls reaching high up to the heavens and white as the fleecy clouds or the rays of the moon, that foremost of cities looked resplendent like Bhogavati... decked with the Nagas.'

statements.claim: Beautifying the place as they went, the Pandavas made it what the storytellers called a second heaven.
statements.evidence: MB 1.209: 'the Pandavas, with Krishna at their head, arriving there, beautified the place and made it a second heaven.'

statements.claim: The city raised on that measured ground came to be known as Indraprastha.
statements.evidence: Pack index title and summary call the established city Indraprastha ('Settles the Pandavas in Indraprastha'), and the epic's own continuation (MB 1.223, used in the sibling packs) speaks of Arjuna reaching 'his own excellent city of Indraprastha'.

statements.claim: When the walls stood, Krishna obtained the Pandavas' leave and set out with Balarama beside him for Dwaraka in the west.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.209: 'And, O monarch, having settled the Pandavas there, the heroic Krishna, obtaining their leave, came back with Rama to Dwaravati.' (Dwaravati = Dwaraka.)

statements.claim: The men of Dwaraka were 'ever engaged in doing what was agreeable and beneficial to Pandu's sons' — the friendship would keep the road between the cities busy.
statements.evidence: Echoes MB 1.209's description of Rama and Krishna ('ever engaged in doing what is agreeable and beneficial to the sons of Pandu'); closing connective.

notes: City-building sequence and Krishna's return with Balarama match MB 1.209 verbatim-level detail. The name Indraprastha is carried by the pack's own index/summary and the epic's continued usage; no contradictions.

statements.claim: Arjuna, in the middle of his forest exile, wandered the sacred waters and holy places on the shores of the western ocean and reached Prabhasa, a sacred and delightful region.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'Arjuna... saw... all the sacred waters and other holy places that were on the shores of the western ocean. Vibhatsu reached the sacred spot called Prabhasa.'

statements.claim: He was 'the invisible Arjuna' — moving quietly, telling no one ahead.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'When the invisible Arjuna arrived at that sacred and delightful region' (the 'invisible' epithet is the text's own).

statements.claim: Krishna, the slayer of Madhu, in Dwaraka, heard of his arrival and went at once to meet him at Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'the slayer of Madhu (Krishna) heard of it. Madhava soon went there to see his friend, the son of Kunti.'

statements.claim: They met and embraced, enquiring after each other's welfare; the text calls them 'dear friends, who were none else than the Rishis Nara and Narayana of old'.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'Krishna and Arjuna met together and embracing each other enquired after each other's welfare. Those dear friends, who were none else than the Rishis Nara and Narayana of old, sat down.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked, 'Why, O Pandava, art thou wandering over the earth, beholding all the sacred waters and other holy places?'; Arjuna told him everything, and Krishna answered, 'This is as it should be.'
statements.evidence: Both quotes verbatim in MB 1.220.

statements.claim: After sporting at Prabhasa as they pleased, they went to the Raivataka mountain to pass some days; at Krishna's command artificers had adorned the mountain and food had been collected in abundance beforehand.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'Krishna and Arjuna having sported as they liked... went to the Raivataka mountain... at the command of Krishna [it] had been well-adorned by many artificers. Much food also had... been collected there.'

statements.claim: Arjuna enjoyed the performances of actors and dancers, dismissed them with respect, lay on an excellent prepared bed describing to Krishna all he had seen — sacred waters, lakes, mountains, rivers, forests — until sleep stole upon him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: full sequence present, ending 'sleep... stole upon him.'

statements.claim: He woke to sweet songs, the melodious notes of the vina and the panegyrics and benedictions of the bards; after the necessary acts and ceremonies Krishna accosted him affectionately and he rode out on a golden car toward Dwaraka, the capital of the Yadavas.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'He rose in the morning, awakened, by sweet songs and melodious notes of the Vina... Riding upon a golden car, the hero then set out for Dwaraka, the capital of the Yadavas.'

statements.claim: At Krishna's command the city of Dwaraka, its gardens and houses, was adorned; citizens poured into the thoroughfares by hundreds of thousands, women mixing with men in the great crowd of Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'for honouring the son of Kunti, the city of Dwaraka was well-adorned, even all the gardens and houses within it... poured eagerly into the public thoroughfares by hundreds of thousands... women, mixing with the men, swelled the great crowd of the Bhojas, the Vrishnis, and the Andhakas.'

statements.claim: Arjuna was welcomed by the sons of the tribes, worshipped those deserving worship, was affectionately received by the young men of the Yadava tribe, repeatedly embraced his age-mates, and stayed many days in Krishna's gem-filled mansion.
statements.evidence: MB 1.220: 'The hero was welcomed with affectionate reception by all the young men of the Yadava tribe... took up his abode there with Krishna for many days.'

notes: Every narrative beat and quotation of this story tracks MB 1.220 closely, including the Nara-Narayana note, the Raivataka arrangements and the Dwaraka reception. Atmosphere (the sea air, the quietness of the invisible wanderer) is unobjectionable connective writing.

statements.claim: When the twelve years of his exile were complete, Arjuna came back to Khandavaprastha with Subhadra, the sister of Krishna, whom he had carried away from Dwaraka and married there.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: Arjuna, stopped by the Vrishnis and brought back, 'was united in marriage with Subhadra'; 'After the twelve years were complete he came back to Khandavaprastha.'

statements.claim: Arjuna approached the king (Yudhishthira) first, then worshipped the brahmanas, and at last went in to Draupadi, who said, 'Why tarriest thou here, O son of Kunti? Go where the daughter of the Satwata race is! A second tie always relaxeth the first one upon a faggot!'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'He approached the king first and then worshipped the Brahmanas... At last the hero went unto Draupadi. Draupadi, from jealousy, spoke unto him...' — quote verbatim.

statements.claim: Arjuna pacified Draupadi repeatedly and asked her forgiveness, then sent Subhadra into the inner apartments dressed not as a queen but in the simple garb of a cowherd woman — his own doing.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'Dhananjaya pacified her repeatedly and asked for her forgiveness. And returning soon unto where Subhadra... was staying, Arjuna, sent her into the inner apartments dressed not as a queen but in the simple garb of a cowherd woman.'

statements.claim: The celebrated Bhadra (Subhadra), of large and slightly red eyes, looked handsomer in that dress; she first worshipped Pritha (Kunti), who from excess of affection smelt her head and pronounced infinite blessings on her.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'the renowned Subhadra looked handsomer in that dress. The celebrated Bhadra of large and slightly red eyes first worshipped Pritha. Kunti from excess of affection smelt the head of that girl... and pronounced infinite blessing upon her.'

statements.claim: Subhadra then hastened to Draupadi, worshipped her and said, 'I am thy maid.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'Then that girl of face like the full moon hastily went unto Draupadi and worshipped her, saying, I am thy maid!'

statements.claim: Draupadi rose quickly and embraced her — the sister of Madhava — from pure affection, and blessed her: 'Let thy husband be without a foe!'; Subhadra answered, 'So be it!'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223 reads 'Krishna rose hastily and embraced the sister of Madhava from affection, and said, Let thy husband be without a foe!' — here Ganguli's 'Krishna' is Krishnā/Draupadi: the same passage uses 'Krishna' for Draupadi two sentences earlier ('And Krishna lamented much in this strain. But Dhananjaya pacified her'), Vasudeva is still at Dwaraka (he arrives only in the next paragraph), and the diacritic KMG edition confirms 'Krishnā rose up hastily and embraced the sister of Mādhava'. Bhadra's reply goes 'unto Draupadi'. Story attribution to Draupadi is correct.

statements.claim: From that time the Pandavas began to live happily, and Kunti too became very happy.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'From that time... those great warriors, the Pandavas, began to live happily, and Kunti also became very happy.'

statements.claim: Hearing Arjuna had reached Indraprastha with his sister, Krishna came with Balarama, the heroes of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes, his brothers and sons and many warriors, with a large army; among them came Akrura (generalissimo of the Vrishni host), Uddhava, Satyaka, Kritavarman, Pradyumna, Gada and many more of the Bhojas and Andhakas, bringing nuptial presents.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'he came thither accompanied by Rama and the other heroes and great warriors of the Vrishni and the Andhaka tribes, and by his brothers and sons...'; Akrura 'the generalissimo of the brave Vrishni host', Uddhava, Satyaka, Kritavarman, Pradyumna, Gada all named; 'bringing with them many nuptial presents.'

statements.claim: King Yudhishthira sent the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, out to receive him, and the Vrishni host entered Khandavaprastha, whose streets were well-swept and watered, decked with floral wreaths and bunches, sprinkled with fragrant sandalwood water, with flags and ensigns flying — every part filled with sweet scent.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'King Yudhishthira, hearing that Madhava had arrived, sent the twins out to receive him. Received by them, the Vrishni host... entered Khandavaprastha well-adorned with flags and ensigns. The streets were well-swept and watered and decked with floral wreaths and bunches. These were... sprinkled over with sandalwood water... Every part of the town was filled with the sweet scent.'

statements.claim: Krishna gave the Pandavas a thousand cars of gold furnished with rows of bells, ten thousand cows, mares and mules, and damsels — nuptial gifts in the manner of a family celebrating a wedding.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223: 'Krishna gave unto the Pandavas a thousand cars of gold furnished with rows of bells... He also gave unto them ten thousand cows'; index summary confirms the full list: 'cars, cows, mares, mules, and damsels as nuptial gifts.'

notes: One delicate spot checked carefully: the embrace and blessing 'Let thy husband be without a foe!' is correctly given to Draupadi (Krishnā), matching MB 1.223 as read with Ganguli's own usage and the diacritic KMG edition. The 'second rope on a faggot' gloss is a fair reading of the simile.

statements.claim: Krishna had come to Indraprastha with the pomp of the Vrishni host — Balarama, Akrura, Uddhava, Satyaka, Kritavarman, his sons and brothers, riding in with nuptial presents while the city was decked with wreaths and sandalwood water.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223 (same passage as DKS_0371's pack): arrival of the Vrishni host and adornment of Khandavaprastha/Indraprastha.

statements.claim: When the celebration was over he stayed: 'the high-souled Vasudeva remained there with Arjuna in the delightful city'.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223 verbatim.

statements.claim: Recap: on first bringing Subhadra home Arjuna faced Draupadi's jealousy ('Why do you tarry here, son of Kunti?... A second tie always relaxes the first one upon a faggot'), pacified her and asked forgiveness, and Subhadra in cowherd garb bowed to Draupadi saying 'I am thy maid.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: all elements present (Draupadi's speech, Arjuna's repeated pacification, the cowherd-garb detail, 'I am thy maid!').

statements.claim: Krishna himself had risen and embraced his sister, and blessed the marriage: 'Let thy husband be without a foe!'
statements.evidence: The pack (MB 1.223) has the actor as Krishnā/Draupadi, not Vasudeva: 'Krishna rose hastily and embraced the sister of Madhava from affection, and said, Let thy husband be without a foe!' — Ganguli uses 'Krishna' for Draupadi throughout this very scene ('And Krishna lamented much in this strain. But Dhananjaya pacified her'), Vasudeva is still in Dwaraka (arriving only in the next paragraph), and the diacritic KMG edition reads 'Krishnā rose up hastily...'. DKS_0371's full account of the same scene correctly attributes the embrace and blessing to Draupadi; Vasudeva 'embraced his sister' is also unsupported by any arrival-scene embrace in the passage.

statements.claim: From that time the household lived happily, and Kunti also became very happy.
statements.evidence: MB 1.223: 'From that time... the Pandavas, began to live happily, and Kunti also became very happy.'

statements.claim: Subhadra, the favourite sister of Kesava, gave birth to an illustrious son, who came to be called Abhimanyu.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223: 'Subhadra, the favourite sister of Kesava, gave birth to an illustrious son... came to be called Abhimanyu.'

statements.claim: Upon Abhimanyu's birth Krishna performed the usual rites of infancy himself; no vision or miracle is recorded — the passage simply tells that the rites were done, and the child grew up like the Moon of the bright fortnight.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt, MB 1.223: 'Upon his birth, Krishna performed the usual rites of infancy. The child began to grow up like the Moon of the bright fortnight.'

statements.claim: The child grew dear to Krishna.
statements.evidence: Pack index summary: 'the child grows dear to him.'

statements.claim: Krishna lingered in the city through the child's earliest years, and when at last he spoke of returning to Dwaraka the parting was a real one.
statements.evidence: Pack records only that Vasudeva 'remained there with Arjuna'; no duration or departure is stated. The continued presence is consistent with the corpus chain (DKS_0373/0374 have Krishna still at Indraprastha), but 'through the child's earliest years' and a narrated departure are unverified closing elaboration.

corrections.original_sentence: Krishna himself had risen and embraced his sister, and blessed the marriage: "Let thy husband be without a foe!"
corrections.suggested: Draupadi herself had risen and embraced her — the sister of Madhava — and blessed the marriage: "Let thy husband be without a foe!"

notes: One CONTRADICTED attribution in the recap of the Subhadra homecoming: MB 1.223 (Ganguli; confirmed by the diacritic KMG edition) has Krishnā/Draupadi rise and embrace Subhadra ('the sister of Madhava') and speak the blessing 'Let thy husband be without a foe!' — Vasudeva was not present at that scene and arrives at Indraprastha only afterwards. The sibling story DKS_0371 tells it correctly. Birth-rites content otherwise fully supported.

statements.claim: Arjuna proposed to Krishna that, the summer days having set in, they go to the banks of the Yamuna and sport with friends, returning in the evening; Krishna said this was his wish too, and with Yudhishthira's leave the two set out surrounded by friends.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: Arjuna's proposal and Krishna's reply quoted; 'Partha and Govinda, with Yudhishthira's leave, set out, surrounded by friends.'

statements.claim: The Pandavas, settled at Indraprastha at the command of Dhritarashtra and Bhishma, brought the neighbouring kings under their sway, and the people lived most happily depending on Yudhishthira the just.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: 'The Pandavas, after they had taken up their abode at Indraprastha at the command of Dhritarashtra and Bhishma began to bring other kings under their sway. All the subjects... lived most happily depending upon Yudhishthira the just.'

statements.claim: Yudhishthira paid homage to virtue, pleasure and profit in judicious proportion as if each were a dear friend; the three pursuits seemed personified on earth with the king shining as a fourth; he was devoted to the Vedas, a performer of the great sacrifices, protector of all good people, and the people delighted in him from sincere affection.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: all these descriptions present nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: They chose a fine Yamuna spot overgrown with tall trees and covered with high mansions that made it look like the celestial city; costly viands and drinks, floral wreaths, perfumes and gem-adorned inner apartments had been gathered there.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: 'Reaching a fine spot... overgrown with numerous tall trees and covered with several high mansions that made the place look like the celestial city... numerous costly and well-flavoured viands and drinks... floral wreaths and various perfumes... inner apartments adorned with many precious gems.'

statements.claim: The women sported as they liked — some in the woods, some in the waters, some within the mansions, as directed by Partha and Govinda; Draupadi and Subhadra, exhilarated with wine, gave away their costly robes and ornaments to the sporting women; some danced, sang, laughed, jested, drank, and obstructed one another in play, while flutes, guitars and kettledrums filled the groves — the scene of Prosperity personified.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: full passage matches, including Draupadi and Subhadra giving away robes and ornaments and the 'scene of Prosperity personified' line.

statements.claim: Arjuna and Vasudeva slipped away to a charming spot a little apart and sat on two very costly seats, discoursing on past achievements of prowess, passing the time like the Aswins seated in heaven.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: 'went to a certain charming spot... sat down upon two very costly seats... discoursing upon many past achievements of prowess... like the Aswins in heaven.'

statements.claim: A certain Brahmana then came to them: he stood like a tall Sala tree, his complexion like molten gold, his beard bright yellow tinged with green, his body in just proportion, his locks matted — a foremost Brahmana blazing with splendour whose coming ended the day's idleness.
statements.evidence: MB 1.224: description verbatim ('looked like a tall Sala tree. His complexion was like unto molten gold; his beard was bright yellow tinged with green; and the height and the thickness of the body were in just proportion. Of matted locks...'); pack excerpt: 'Beholding that foremost of Brahmanas blazing with splendour approach...'

notes: All claims mirror MB 1.224 closely. Sensory embellishments around the Brahmana's approach (the grove growing quieter) are atmospheric connective writing, not factual assertions.

statements.claim: The Brahmana asked Arjuna and Vasudeva for food as a starving man: 'I am a voracious Brahmana that always eateth much... I solicit you to gratify me by giving me sufficient food'; they answered they would, asking what food would gratify him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: both speeches verbatim.

statements.claim: He revealed: 'I do not desire to eat ordinary food. Know that I am Agni! Give me that food which suiteth me.'
statements.evidence: MB 1.225 verbatim.

statements.claim: Agni explained that the Khandava forest is always protected by Indra, so he always fails to consume it; the Naga Takshaka, Indra's friend, dwells there with his followers and family, and Indra pours water from the clouds whenever Agni blazes forth; he asked the two weapon-skilled heroes to prevent the showers from descending and to stop any creature from escaping when he begins to consume the forest.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: Agni's whole speech quoted in the pack matches the story nearly verbatim.

statements.claim: Agni called them 'the two foremost of heroes on earth'.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: 'Ye who are now staying so near unto Khandava are the two foremost of heroes on earth.'

statements.claim: At Janamejaya's question why Agni desired the forest, Vaisampayana narrated the tale told by the Rishis in the Purana: king Swetaki, endued with strength and prowess, equal to Indra, unequalled on earth in sacrifices, charity and intelligence, performed the five great sacrifices and many others year after year with large presents, until the sacrificial priests, eyes afflicted by the continued smoke and bodies grown weak, left him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: 'I will narrate to you the story of the conflagration of Khandava as told by Rishis in the Purana... there was a celebrated king of the name of Swetaki... equal unto Indra himself... till those sacrificial priests with eyes afflicted by the continued smoke and becoming very weak, left that monarch.'

statements.claim: Swetaki, refused by the priests for a proposed hundred-year sacrifice despite courting them with bowing, conciliatory speeches and gifts of wealth, warned them that if abandoned from enmity or improper motive he would seek other priests, representing his business to them.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: the king's warning is quoted almost verbatim ('If you abandon me from enmity alone or any improper motive, I shall go unto other priests... and conciliating them by sweet words and gifts, I shall represent unto them the business I have on hand').

statements.claim: The priests, knowing they could not assist at the king's sacrifice, pretended to be angry in their turn: 'Thy sacrifices are incessant,' they told him.
statements.evidence: MB 1.225: 'when those priests well knew that they could not assist at the king's sacrifice, they pretended to be angry, and addressing... said, O best of kings, thy sacrifices are incessan[t]...' (pack passage truncated mid-word but opening matches exactly).

notes: Agni's request and the opening of the Swetaki tale match MB 1.225 closely, with dialogue quoted nearly verbatim. Frame prose (the summer air, the forest kept unburned 'so long') is connective; the pack's own truncation ends mid-Swetaki-tale, and the story likewise pauses there.

statements.claim: Hearing that the Pandavas had been banished, the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas went to the great forest (Kamyaka) where the brothers lived in affliction, joined by the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and the celebrated Kaikeya brothers; reproaching the sons of Dhritarashtra, they asked 'What should we do?'
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 verbatim; pack index fixes the location as the Kamyaka forest.

statements.claim: The bulls of the Kshatriya race, with Vasudeva at their head, sat down in a ring around Yudhishthira the just; saluting that foremost of the Kurus respectfully, Kesava spoke mournfully.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'And those bulls of the Kshatriya race, with Vasudeva at their head, sat themselves down round Yudhishthira the just. And respectfully saluting that foremost of the Kurus, Kesava mournfully said...'

statements.claim: Krishna's vow: 'The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni! Slaying these in battle and defeating their followers along with their royal allies, will we all install Yudhishthira the just on the throne! The wicked deserve to be slain! Verily, this is eternal morality.'
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 verbatim (also the pack's excerpt).

statements.claim: Speaking of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Krishna got into a passion and seemed bent upon consuming all created things; Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him by reciting the feats Krishna achieved in his former lives — the soul of all things, immeasurable, the eternal one of infinite energy, the lord of Prajapati, the supreme ruler of the worlds, Vishnu of profound wisdom.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: 'when on account of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Janardana had thus got into a passion, and seemed bent upon consuming all created things, Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him... began to recite the feats achieved in his former lives by that soul of all things...'

statements.claim: The recited ascetic feats: ten thousand years as a muni on the Gandhamadana mountains; eleven thousand years living on water alone by the lake of Pushkara; a hundred years on one leg on the high hills of Vadari living on air; twelve years of emaciated sacrifice on the banks of the Saraswati; a thousand years of the celestials standing on one leg on the plains of Prabhasa.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: all five feats with the same numbers present verbatim.

statements.claim: The recited deeds: slaying the Asura Naraka (offspring of the Earth), taking his ear-rings, performing the first horse-sacrifice with Naraka as the victim; slaying the Daityas and Danavas and giving Indra the sovereignty of the universe; slaying Ahvriti at Jaruthi, Kratha, Sisupala with his adherents, Jarasandha, Saivya and Satadhanwan; defeating Rukmi in battle and obtaining the daughter of Bhoja for queen; slaying Indradyumna, the Yavana Kaseruman and Salwa the lord of Saubha and destroying the city of Saubha; and as a child filling heaven, the firmament and the earth in three steps.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12: every item in Arjuna's recitation appears in the pack passage with matching detail.

statements.claim: As Arjuna recited, Krishna's wrath, which had seemed bent on consuming all created things, began to be held; yet the anger was not fully turned aside and Arjuna's words had not yet done their full work.
statements.evidence: MB 3.12 shows only the start of the pacification ('Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him... began to recite'); the completion belongs to the next corpus beat (DKS_0376 'Arjuna Pacifies the Wrathful Krishna'). The story's hedged phrasing stays within that arc — connective staging rather than an asserted sourceable outcome.

notes: Vow, visiting kinsmen, and Arjuna's litany of Krishna's former-life feats and slayings all match MB 3.12 in near-verbatim detail, including every number. Only the closing note that the wrath 'began to be held' is a connective bridge to the next story.
